sentences.text: Brachytrachelopan was a small sauropod dinosaur, reaching a total length of 10 to 11 meters and weighing about 5 metric tons.
Its neck vertebrae were unique because they were as long as or shorter than they were high, and they showed a strongly opisthocoelous form.
The neck was approximately 40 percent shorter than in other dicraeosaurids, consisting of only 12 vertebrae with an estimated length of 1.1 meters.
The longest vertebral centrum measured just 10 centimeters.
The spine featured complex structures including a prespinal plate and various laminae alongside shorter spinodiapophysial processes.
This animal breaks supposed sauropod rules by being small and having a notably short neck compared to its relatives.
The genus name translates to Short-necked Pan, honoring the shepherd who found it and highlighting its short neck.
The only known specimen was found in the Cañadón Calcáreo Formation, about 25 km north-northeast of Cerro Cóndor in Chubut Province, Argentina.
Daniel Mesa, a local shepherd looking for lost sheep, discovered the fossil and marked the spot with a stake.
The research team was led by German paleontologist Oliver Rauhut, working with Argentines Gerardo Cladera and Pablo Puerta.
Researchers determined the specimen was an adult, not a juvenile, based on the high degree of fusion between neural arches and centra.
The neck structure suggests it specialized in eating plants growing at heights between 1 and 2 meters and may have been very selective in choosing its food.
Brachytrachelopan is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae, the group Diplodocoidea, the suborder Neosauropoda, and the parent group Dicraeosaurinae.
Rauhut and colleagues proposed that Brachytrachelopan is more closely related to the Late Jurassic African Dicraeosaurus than to the Lower Cretaceous South American Amargasaurus.
Brachytrachelopan lived in Argentina during the Late Jurassic, specifically from the Oxfordian to Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 145.06 million years ago.
The geological formation containing fossils consists of river sediments with evidence of lakes and swamps, where dominant plants included Classopollis, Callialasporites, and Cyclusphaera.
Researchers suggest that due to its neck length, it may have had a very different lifestyle from those with longer necks, occupying an ecological niche not filled by its infraorder companions.
While a hypothesis links sauropod neck elongation to sexual selection, this view is refuted by other authors.
